items.title: Caste is a complex social hierarchy with religious framings
items.claim: How does the caste system relate to Hindu religion?

options.text: It is purely social with no religious dimension

Varna (the fourfold theoretical division — Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) is described in the Vedas and the Manusmriti; jati (thousands of birth-based occupational groupings) is the lived reality; modern reform movements (Ambedkar, Gandhi, contemporary Dalit activism) have contested its religious basis
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

Dalits (formerly 'untouchables') were treated as outside the varna system. B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex. Caste discrimination persists in many forms — the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a religious tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) has three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). Tanakh is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in a one-year cycle (annual cycle) or three-year cycle (some Reform congregations). The annual cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' as a generic term for Jewish scripture obscures structure. Students need to distinguish Torah, Tanakh and Talmud — and notice that Christian 'Old Testament' is the same content as Tanakh but in different order.

items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began over political succession in 632 CE
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two separate communities formed centuries apart in different countries

After Muhammad's death on 8 June 632 CE without a clear successor, those who supported Abu Bakr (chosen as first caliph) became Sunni; those who held Ali (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) had been designated became Shia — entrenched after Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE

items.reveal:
Abu Bakr was chosen at Saqifah immediately after Muhammad's death. Umar (634-644), Uthman (644-656), then Ali (656-661) followed as the 'Rightly-Guided Caliphs'. Umar and Uthman were assassinated.

The First Fitna (civil war, 656-661) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. Husayn's grandfather was Muhammad; his death is mourned annually at Ashura.

Globally, around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Major religious traditions can be shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.
